title: Buffett on intrinsic value
lede: Buffett calls intrinsic value the number that matters, while accepting that nobody can fix it exactly. Across six decades, the letters describe it as future cash discounted to today, show why book value was only a proxy that he later dropped, acknowledge that he and Munger could reach different answers, and explain how the estimate sets what he will pay, including for Berkshire's own shares.

entries.excerpt: …widespread public belief in the inevitability of profits from investment in stocks will lead to eventual trouble. Should this occur, prices, but not intrinsic values in my opinion, of even undervalued securities can be expected to be substantially affected
entries.note: In the partnership years, price and value were already separate amounts. A crash changes the first, not the second.

entries.excerpt: It probably also is fair to say that the quoted book value in 1964 somewhat overstated the intrinsic value of the enterprise, since the assets owned at that time on either a going concern basis or a liquidating value basis were not worth 100 cents on the dollar.
entries.note: He admits that 1964 book value made the business look better than it was. The proxy can understate or overstate value.

entries.excerpt: Intrinsic business value is an economic concept, estimating future cash output discounted to present value. Book value tells you what has been put in; intrinsic business value estimates what can be taken out.
entries.note: The definition appears in the same letter explaining that book value only stands in for it.

entries.excerpt: If the financial experience of new owners of Berkshire is merely to match the future financial experience of the company, any premium of market value over intrinsic business value that they pay must be maintained.
entries.note: He applies it to Berkshire's own shares after they had moved from a discount to an occasional premium.

entries.excerpt: Indeed, if you aren't certain that you understand and can value your business far better than Mr. Market, you don't belong in the game.
entries.note: Graham's Mr. Market allegory appeared in early 1988, after the October crash. Valuation skill provides the entry ticket.

entries.excerpt: With perfect foresight, this number can be calculated by taking all future cash flows of a business - in and out - and discounting them at prevailing interest rates. So valued, all businesses, from manufacturers of buggy whips to operators of cellular phones, become economic equals.
entries.note: The discounted-cash-flow definition uses one yardstick for every industry, so unlike businesses can be compared.

entries.excerpt: Berkshire's intrinsic value continues to exceed book value by a substantial margin. We can't tell you the exact differential because intrinsic value is necessarily an estimate; Charlie and I might, in fact, differ by 10% in our appraisals.
entries.note: The estimate varies by person. He states how much he and Munger might differ.

entries.excerpt: If we calculate the value of a common stock to be only slightly higher than its price, we're not interested in buying. We believe this margin-of-safety principle, so strongly emphasized by Ben Graham, to be the cornerstone of investment success.
entries.note: Margin of safety links the estimate to price as the operating rule, and he credits Graham for it.

entries.excerpt: Anyone calculating intrinsic value necessarily comes up with a highly subjective figure that will change both as estimates of future cash flows are revised and as interest rates move.
entries.note: Interest rates enter the definition directly. Higher rates make the same business worth less.

entries.excerpt: Therefore, the offering we propose will not diminish the per-share intrinsic value of our existing stock. Let me also put our thoughts about valuation more baldly: Berkshire is selling at a price at which Charlie and I would not consider buying it.
entries.note: When he issued the B shares, he told prospective buyers directly that the stock was not cheap on his own yardstick.

entries.excerpt: Charlie and I admit that we feel confident in estimating intrinsic value for only a portion of traded equities and then only when we employ a range of values, rather than some pseudo-precise figure.
entries.note: He wrote this as buybacks came into fashion. He used a range, not a single estimate, and only for businesses he could read.

entries.excerpt: I say “estimate” because calculations of intrinsic value, though all-important, are necessarily imprecise and often seriously wrong. The more uncertain the future of a business, the more possibility there is that the calculation will be wildly off-base.
entries.note: The caveat opens a letter split into four groups, so readers can estimate Berkshire for themselves.

entries.excerpt: The challenge, of course, is the calculation of intrinsic value. Present that task to Charlie and me separately, and you will get two different answers. Precision just isn’t possible.
entries.note: He finally states the disagreement openly, twenty years after the ten per cent admission.

entries.excerpt: We have no way to pinpoint intrinsic value. But we do have a useful, though considerably understated, proxy for it: per-share book value. This yardstick is meaningless at most companies. At Berkshire, however, book value very roughly tracks business values.
entries.note: He defends book value as a scorecard only because its gap from intrinsic value stays roughly stable at Berkshire.

entries.excerpt: By our estimate, a 120%-of-book price is a significant discount to Berkshire’s intrinsic value, a spread that is appropriate because calculations of intrinsic value can’t be precise.
entries.note: He explains the 120%-of-book buyback ceiling. The gap below intrinsic value allows for error in the estimate.

entries.excerpt: The math of such purchases is simple: Each transaction makes per-share intrinsic value go up, while per-share book value goes down. That combination causes the book-value scorecard to become increasingly out of touch with economic reality.
entries.note: He dropped book value as the headline metric after nearly three decades. Buybacks above book had made the proxy misleading.
